arXiv:0710.2233v2 [nlin.SI] 11 Aug 2008

Global classification of two-component approximately integrable evolution equations

Peter H. van der Kamp
Department of Mathematics,
La Trobe University, Victoria, 3086, Australia
Email: P.vanderkamp@latrobe.edu.au
Abstract

We globally classify two-component evolution equations, with homogeneous diagonal linear part, admitting infinitely many approximate symmetries. Important ingredients are the symbolic calculus of Gel’fand and Dikiĭ, the Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem, results on diophantine equations in roots of unity by F. Beukers, and an algorithm of C.J. Smyth.

1 Introduction

A long standing open problem is the classification, up to linear transformations, of two-component integrable equations

(utvt)=(a​un+F⁡(u,v,u1,v1,…)b​vn+G⁡(u,v,u1,v1,…))\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}au_{n}+F(u,v,u_{1},v_{1},\ldots)\\ bv_{n}+G(u,v,u_{1},v_{1},\ldots)\end{array}\right) (1)

where F,GF,G are purely nonlinear polynomials in variables ui,viu_{i},v_{i}, which denote the ii-th xx-derivatives of u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t)u(x,t),v(x,t). Among the many different approaches to recognition and classification of integrable equations, the so called symmetry approach has proven to be particularly successful, see for example [25, 40] and references in there. Until recently, all results obtained were for classes of equations at fixed (low) order nn. This situation changed dramatically when, by using a symbolic calculus and results from number theory, Sanders and Wang classified scalar evolution equations with respect to symmetries globally, that is, where the order nn can be arbitrarily high [34]. Our aim is to obtain a similar result for the class of multi-component equations (1).

In the symmetry approach the existence of infinitely many generalized symmetries is taken as the definition of integrability. A generalized symmetry of equation (1) is a pair of differential polynomials S=(S1,S2)S=(S_{1},S_{2}) such that equation (1) is also satisfied by u~=u+ϵ​S1\tilde{u}=u+\epsilon S_{1}, v~=v+ϵ​S2\tilde{v}=v+\epsilon S_{2} up to order ϵ2\epsilon^{2}. This leads to the notion of Lie-derivative: ℒ⁡(K)​S=0{\mathcal{L}}(K)S=0 ⇔\Leftrightarrow SS is a symmetry of (ut,vt)=K(u_{t},v_{t})=K.

The Lie algebra of pairs of differential polynomials is a graded algebra. The linear part (a​un,b​vn)(au_{n},bv_{n}) has total grading 00, the quadratic terms have total grading 11, and so on. Gradings are used to divide the condition for the existence of a symmetry into a number of simpler conditions: ℒ⁡(K)​S≡0{\mathcal{L}}(K)S\equiv 0 modulo quadratic terms, ℒ⁡(K)​S≡0{\mathcal{L}}(K)S\equiv 0 modulo cubic terms, and so on. This has been called the perturbative symmetry approach [21]. In the same spirit the idea of an approximate symmetry was defined [23]. If ℒ⁡(K)​S≡0{\mathcal{L}}(K)S\equiv 0 modulo cubic terms, we say that SS is an approximate symmetry of degree 2. And, we call an equation approximately integrable if it has infinitely many approximate symmetries.

We contribute to the above mentioned problem by globally classifying equations (1) that are approximately integrable of degree 2. This is achieved by applying the techniques developed in the special case of so called ℬ{\mathcal{B}}-equations, where any approximate symmetry of degree 2 is a genuine symmetry [12]. It extends older results obtained by Beukers, Sanders and Wang [2, 3]. See [17] for an overview on the application of number theory in the analysis of integrable evolution equations and [24] for more recent results. The present article is a revised and extended version of the report [13].

As remarked in [23] the requirement of the existence of approximate symmetries of degree 22 is very restrictive and highly non-trivial. On the other hand an equation may have infinitely many approximate symmetries of degree 22, but fail to have any symmetries. This problem involves conditions of higher grading and is left open.

2 Generalized symmetries

A symmetry-group transforms one solution to an equation to another solution of the same equation. We refer to the book of Olver [29] for an introduction to the subject, numerous examples and applications.

We denote 𝒜=ℂ⁡[u,v,u1,v1,…]{\mathcal{A}}=\mathbb{C}[u,v,u_{1},v_{1},\ldots] and 𝔤=𝒜⊗𝒜{\mathfrak{g}}={\mathcal{A}}\otimes{\mathcal{A}}. We will endow 𝔤{\mathfrak{g}} with the structure of a Lie algebra. For any K=(K1,K2)∈𝔤K=(K_{1},K_{2})\in{\mathfrak{g}} the pair S=(S1,S2)∈𝔤S=(S_{1},S_{2})\in{\mathfrak{g}} is a generalized symmetry of the two-component evolution equation

(utvt)=(K1K2)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}K_{1}\\ K_{2}\end{array}\right) (2)

if the Lie derivative of SS with respect to KK,

ℒ⁡(K)​S=(δK​(S1)−δS​(K1)δK​(S2)−δS​(K2)),{\mathcal{L}}(K)S=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\delta_{K}(S_{1})-\delta_{S}(K_{1})\\ \delta_{K}(S_{2})-\delta_{S}(K_{2})\end{array}\right), (3)

vanishes. Here δQ\delta_{Q} is the prolongation of the evolutionary vector field with characteristic QQ, cf. [29, equation 5.6],

δ(Q1,Q2)=∑k=0∞Dxk​Q1​∂∂uk+Dxk​Q2​∂∂vk,\delta_{(Q_{1},Q_{2})}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}D_{x}^{k}Q_{1}\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{k}}+D_{x}^{k}Q_{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial v_{k}},

and the total derivative DxD_{x} is11 1 In [17, section 4.1] the total derivative was denoted δx\delta_{x}. This is misleading as Dx=δ(u1,v1)D_{x}=\delta_{(u_{1},v_{1})}. Also δQ\delta_{Q} is the unique ℂ\mathbb{C}-linear derivation on 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} satisfying δQ​(u,v)=Q\delta_{Q}(u,v)=Q and δQ∘Dx=Dx∘δQ\delta_{Q}\circ D_{x}=D_{x}\circ\delta_{Q}.

Dx=∑k=0∞uk+1​∂∂uk+vk+1​∂∂vk.D_{x}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}u_{k+1}\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{k}}+v_{k+1}\frac{\partial}{\partial v_{k}}.

The Lie derivative is a representation of 𝔤{\mathfrak{g}}. This property, with P,Q∈𝔤P,Q\in{\mathfrak{g}},

ℒ⁡(ℒ⁡(P)​Q)=ℒ⁡(P)​ℒ​(Q)−ℒ⁡(Q)​ℒ​(P){\mathcal{L}}({\mathcal{L}}(P)Q)={\mathcal{L}}(P){\mathcal{L}}(Q)-{\mathcal{L}}(Q){\mathcal{L}}(P) (4)

corresponds to the Jacobi identity for the Lie bracket [P,Q]=ℒ⁡(P)​Q[P,Q]={\mathcal{L}}(P)Q which is clearly bilinear and antisymmetric, cf. [29, Proposition 5.15]. Another way of expressing (4) is saying that 𝔤{\mathfrak{g}} is a 𝔤{\mathfrak{g}}-module. Another 𝔤{\mathfrak{g}}-module is given by 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, the representation being ℒ​(K)​F=δK​(F){\mathcal{L}}(K)F=\delta_{K}(F) with K∈𝔤,F∈𝒜K\in{\mathfrak{g}},F\in{\mathcal{A}}.

The word ‘generalized’ stresses the fact that the order of a symmetry can be bigger than one. Generally symmetries come in hierarchies with periodic gaps between their orders. For example, the Korteweg–De Vries equation ut=u3+u​u1u_{t}=u_{3}+uu_{1} possesses odd order symmetries only. Concurrently, the KDV equation has approximately symmetries at any order.

3 Grading

Denote σu=(u,0)\sigma_{u}=(u,0) and σv=(0,v)\sigma_{v}=(0,v). If PP in some 𝔤{\mathfrak{g}}-module is an eigenvector of ℒ⁡(σu){\mathcal{L}}(\sigma_{u}) (or of ℒ⁡(σv){\mathcal{L}}(\sigma_{v})), the corresponding eigenvalue is called the uu- (or vv-) grading of PP. If PP has uu-grading ii and vv-grading jj we say that i+ji+j is the total grading of PP. One verifies that 𝔤{\mathfrak{g}} can be written as the direct sum

𝔤=⨁t≥0𝔤t,𝔤t=⨁−1≤i≤t+1𝔤i,t−i,{\mathfrak{g}}=\bigoplus_{t\geq 0}{\mathfrak{g}}^{t},\quad{\mathfrak{g}}^{t}=\bigoplus_{-1\leq i\leq t+1}{\mathfrak{g}}^{i,t-i},

where elements of 𝔤i,j{\mathfrak{g}}^{i,j} have uu-grading ii and vv-grading jj. For example, (u1​v2,v3​v4)∈𝔤0,1(u_{1}v_{2},v_{3}v_{4})\in{\mathfrak{g}}^{0,1} has total grading 1. Similarly we have

𝒜=⨁t≥0𝒜t,𝒜t=⨁0≤i≤t𝒜i,t−i.{\mathcal{A}}=\bigoplus_{t\geq 0}{\mathcal{A}}^{t},\quad{\mathcal{A}}^{t}=\bigoplus_{0\leq i\leq t}{\mathcal{A}}^{i,t-i}.

The crucial property of a graded Lie algebra is that the uu-, (or vv-, or total) grading of ℒ⁡(P)​Q{\mathcal{L}}(P)Q is the sum of the uu-, (or vv-, or total) gradings of PP and QQ. This follows directly from equation (4). Gradings are used to divide the condition for the existence of a symmetry into a number of simpler conditions.

We study evolution equations of the form

(utvt)\displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right) =\displaystyle= K0+K1+⋯\displaystyle K^{0}+K^{1}+\cdots (8)
=\displaystyle= K0,0+K−1,2+K0,1+K1,0+K2,−1+⋯,\displaystyle K^{0,0}+K^{-1,2}+K^{0,1}+K^{1,0}+K^{2,-1}+\cdots,

with K0,0=(a​un,b​vn)K^{0,0}=(au_{n},bv_{n}) and symmetries of similar form S=S0+S1+⋯S=S^{0}+S^{1}+\cdots with S0=S0,0=(c​um,d​vm)S^{0}=S^{0,0}=(cu_{m},dv_{m}).22 2 We remark that only if a=ba=b then SS may also contain terms S±1,∓1S^{\pm 1,\mp 1}. In this paper we implicitly assume this does not happen. Here the dots may contain terms with total grading >1>1. Certainly we have ℒ⁡(K0,0)​S0,0=0{\mathcal{L}}(K^{0,0})S^{0,0}=0. The symmetry conditions with total grading 1 are

ℒ⁡(K−1,2)​S0,0+ℒ⁡(K0,0)​S−1,2\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}(K^{-1,2})S^{0,0}+{\mathcal{L}}(K^{0,0})S^{-1,2} =0,\displaystyle=0, (9)
ℒ⁡(K0,0)​S0,1+ℒ⁡(K0,1)​S0,0\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}(K^{0,0})S^{0,1}+{\mathcal{L}}(K^{0,1})S^{0,0} =0,\displaystyle=0,
ℒ⁡(K0,0)​S1,0+ℒ⁡(K1,0)​S0,0\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}(K^{0,0})S^{1,0}+{\mathcal{L}}(K^{1,0})S^{0,0} =0,\displaystyle=0,
ℒ⁡(K0,0)​S2,−1+ℒ⁡(K2,−1)​S0,0\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}(K^{0,0})S^{2,-1}+{\mathcal{L}}(K^{2,-1})S^{0,0} =0.\displaystyle=0.

An implicit function theorem which, under certain conditions, guarantees that SS is a symmetry of KK if the first few symmetry conditions of total grading 0,1,…0,1,\ldots are fulfilled, was given by Sanders and Wang [34, 35]. In this paper we restrict ourselves to solving equations (9). Thus we classify equations that admit infinitely many approximate symmetries of degree 2, which is a necessary condition for integrability. In the sequel we omit the adjective ‘of degree 2’.

4 The Gel’fand–Dikiĭ transformation

Comparing the Leibniz rule and Newton’s binomial formula,

(u​v)n=∑i=0n(ni)​ui​vn−i,(x+y)n=∑i=0n(ni)​xi​yn−i,(uv)_{n}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}u_{i}v_{n-i},\qquad(x+y)^{n}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}x^{i}y^{n-i},

we see that differentiating a product is quite similar to taking the power of a sum. On the right hand side the index, counting the number of derivatives, gets interchanged with the power, while on the left hand side differentiation becomes multiplying with the sum of symbols. Of course, with expressions containing both indices and powers, one has to be more careful. The Gel’fand–Dikiĭ transformation [10] provides a one to one correspondence between 𝒜i,j{\mathcal{A}}^{i,j} and the space ℂi,j\mathbb{C}^{i,j}: polynomials in ℂ⁡[x1,…,xi,y1,…,yj]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{i},y_{1},\ldots,y_{j}] that are symmetric in both the xx and the yy symbols. One may deduce the general rule from

u1​u2​v3​⊵​x11​x22+x21​x122!​y131!=u1​u2​v3^,u_{1}u_{2}v_{3}\trianglerighteq\frac{x_{1}^{1}x_{2}^{2}+x_{2}^{1}x_{1}^{2}}{2!}\frac{y_{1}^{3}}{1!}=\widehat{u_{1}u_{2}v_{3}},

or consult one of the papers [17, 21, 24]. All usual operations from differential algebra translate naturally. In particular,33 3 As a correction to [17, Section 4.3], when (f,g)∈𝔤i,j(f,g)\in{\mathfrak{g}}^{i,j} then f∈𝒜i+1,jf\in{\mathcal{A}}^{i+1,j} and g∈𝒜i,j+1g\in{\mathcal{A}}^{i,j+1}. One should think of (f,g)(f,g) as representing the vector field f∂u+g∂vf\partial_{u}+g\partial_{v}.

ℒ⁡(K0,0)​Si,j​⊵​(𝒢1;ni,j​[a,b]00𝒢2;ni,j​[a,b])​Si,j^,{\mathcal{L}}(K^{0,0})S^{i,j}\trianglerighteq\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}{\mathcal{G}}^{i,j}_{1;n}[a{,}b]&0\\ 0&{\mathcal{G}}^{i,j}_{2;n}[a{,}b]\end{array}\right)\widehat{S^{i,j}},

where the so called 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}-functions are given by

𝒢1;ni,j​[a,b]​(x,y)\displaystyle{\mathcal{G}}^{i,j}_{1;n}[a{,}b](x,y) =\displaystyle= a⁡(x1n+⋯+xi+1n)+b⁡(y1n+⋯+yjn)\displaystyle a(x_{1}^{n}+\cdots+x_{i+1}^{n})+b(y_{1}^{n}+\cdots+y_{j}^{n})
−a​(x1+⋯+xi+1+y1+⋯+yj)n,\displaystyle-a(x_{1}+\cdots+x_{i+1}+y_{1}+\cdots+y_{j})^{n},

and

𝒢2;ni,j​[a,b]​(x,y)=𝒢1;nj,i​[b,a]​(y,x).{\mathcal{G}}^{i,j}_{2;n}[a{,}b](x,y)={\mathcal{G}}^{j,i}_{1;n}[b{,}a](y,x). (10)

Symbolically we can solve the symmetry conditions of total grading 1, equations (9), as follows. We may write the components of the quadratic parts of SS as, with k=1,2k=1,2,

Ski,j^=𝒢k;mi,j​[c,d]𝒢k;ni,j​[a,b]​Kki,j^.\widehat{S^{i,j}_{k}}=\frac{{\mathcal{G}}^{i,j}_{k;m}[c{,}d]}{{\mathcal{G}}^{i,j}_{k;n}[a{,}b]}\widehat{K^{i,j}_{k}}. (11)

Equation (8) has an approximate symmetry at order mm with linear coefficients c,dc,d iff for all i+j=1i+j=1 and k=1,2k=1,2 the right hand side of equation (11) is either polynomial or undefined (0/00/0).

5 Nonlinear injectivity

In our classification we distinguish between equations whose approximate symmetries necessarily have non-vanishing linear part and equations that allow purely nonlinear approximate symmetries.

Definition 1

Let K0K^{0} have total grading 0. We call K0K^{0} nonlinear injective if ℒ⁡(K0)​S=0{\mathcal{L}}(K^{0})S=0 implies that SS has total grading 0. And, we call an equation nonlinear injective if its linear part is nonlinear injective.

With K0=(a​un,b​vn)K^{0}=(au_{n},bv_{n}), the kk-th component of ℒ⁡(K0)​Si,j{\mathcal{L}}(K^{0})S^{i,j}, with non-zero Si,jS^{i,j}, vanishes iff 𝒢k,ni,j​[a,b]=0{\mathcal{G}}^{i,j}_{k,n}[a{,}b]=0. Solving the later equation with i+j=1i+j=1 yields a​b=0ab=0, n≥0n\geq 0, or n=1n=1, or (a−2​b)​(2​a−b)=0(a-2b)(2a-b)=0, n=0n=0. In Table 1 we have displayed all K0K^{0} and corresponding S1S^{1}, such that the equation (ut,vt)=K0+K1(u_{t},v_{t})=K^{0}+K^{1}, with arbitrary K1∈𝔤1K^{1}\in{\mathfrak{g}}^{1}, has purely nonlinear approximate symmetries S1∈𝔤1S^{1}\in{\mathfrak{g}}^{1}. Note that the classification is performed up to linear transformations. In particular we may interchange uu and vv. Therefore without loss of generality we set b=1b=1 and classify the values of aa up till inversion.

For the same choices of K0K^{0} and S1S^{1} the linear equation (ut,vt)=K0(u_{t},v_{t})=K^{0} has symmetries (c​um,d​vm)+S1(cu_{m},dv_{m})+S^{1} for all m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} and c,d∈ℂc,d\in\mathbb{C}. Indeed, every ℬ{\mathcal{B}}-equation, that is, an equation of the form (8) with K1∈𝔤−1,2K^{1}\in{\mathfrak{g}}^{-1,2}, admits the zeroth order symmetry (2​u,v)(2u,v). In fact, every tuple S∈𝔤S\in{\mathfrak{g}} is a symmetry of (ut,vt)=(u1,v1)(u_{t},v_{t})=(u_{1},v_{1}). Or, in other words, (u1,v1)(u_{1},v_{1}) is a symmetry of every equation.

Only a subset of the equations (ut,vt)=K0+K1(u_{t},v_{t})=K^{0}+K^{1}, with particular K1∈𝔤K^{1}\in{\mathfrak{g}}, has infinitely many symmetries with non-vanishing linear part. There is a good reason for including such equations in the classification: their approximate symmetries may correspond to approximately integrable nonlinear injective equations. One integrable example, equation (40), is given in section 11. On the other hand, nonlinear injectivity is one of the conditions in the implicit function theorem of Sanders and Wang, see section 3.

6 Necessary and sufficient conditions

In this section we introduce convenient notation, we give necessary and sufficient conditions for a nonlinear injective equation to be approximately integrable, and we outline how we perform the classification.

The components of equation (8) are

(utvt)=(a​un+K11,0+K10,1+K1−1,2+⋯b​vn+K20,1+K21,0+K22,−1+⋯).\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}au_{n}+K_{1}^{1,0}+K_{1}^{0,1}+K_{1}^{-1,2}+\cdots\\ bv_{n}+K_{2}^{0,1}+K_{2}^{1,0}+K_{2}^{2,-1}+\cdots\end{array}\right). (12)

We denote the symbolic representation of the 6-tuple K11,0K_{1}^{1,0}, K10,1K_{1}^{0,1}, K1−1,2K_{1}^{-1,2}, K20,1K_{2}^{0,1}, K21,0K_{2}^{1,0}, K22,−1K_{2}^{2,-1} by K^1\widehat{K}^{1}. And similarly we write S11,0S_{1}^{1,0}, …\ldots, S22,−1​⊵​S^1S_{2}^{2,-1}\trianglerighteq\widehat{S}^{1} and 𝒢n=𝒢1;n1,0,…,𝒢2;n2,−1{\mathcal{G}}_{n}={\mathcal{G}}_{1;n}^{1,0},\ldots,{\mathcal{G}}_{2;n}^{2,-1}. A 66-tuple HH is called proper if it consists of polynomials with the right symmetry properties, that is, if H∈ℂ2,0⊗ℂ1,1⊗ℂ0,2⊗ℂ0,2⊗ℂ1,1⊗ℂ2,0H\in\mathbb{C}^{2,0}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{1,1}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{0,2}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{0,2}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{1,1}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{2,0}. Thus, K^1\widehat{K}^{1}, S^1\widehat{S}^{1}, and 𝒢n​[a,b]{\mathcal{G}}_{n}[a{,}b] are proper tuples. We will also consider ss-tuples, with s<6s<6. It should be clear from the context in which space a proper ss-tuple lives. We say that an ss-tuple H=H[1],…,H[s]H=H_{[1]},\ldots,H_{[s]} divides an ss-tuple P=P[1],…,P[s]P=P_{[1]},\ldots,P_{[s]} if H[i]|P[i]H_{[i]}\mid P_{[i]} for all 1≤i≤s1\leq i\leq s and we write P/H=P[1]/H[1],…,P[s]/H[s]P/H=P_{[1]}/H_{[1]},\ldots,P_{[s]}/H_{[s]}. We are now able to state the following: Equation (12) is nonlinear injective and has an approximate symmetry of order mm with linear coefficients c,dc,d iff the 6-tuple S^1=𝒢m​[c,d]​K^1/𝒢n​[a,b]\widehat{S}^{1}={\mathcal{G}}_{m}[c{,}d]\widehat{K}^{1}/{\mathcal{G}}_{n}[a{,}b] is proper.

Let HH, 𝒢m​[c,d]{\mathcal{G}}_{m}[c,d] be proper ss-tuples. With m⁡(H)m(H) we denote the set of all m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} such that there exists c,d∈ℂc,d\in\mathbb{C} for which H|𝒢m​[c,d]H\mid{\mathcal{G}}_{m}[c{,}d]. And, the set of all proper ss-tuples HH with infinite m⁡(H)m(H) will be denoted ℋs{\mathcal{H}}^{s}, or simply ℋ{\mathcal{H}} when it is clear from the context what ss is. We organize H∈ℋH\in{\mathcal{H}} by the lowest order nn at which HH divides a 𝒢n{\mathcal{G}}_{n}-tuple. By ℋn{\mathcal{H}}_{n} we denote the set of all proper tuples HH with infinite m⁡(H)m(H) whose smallest element is nn.

We have the following lemma.

Lemma 2

Equation (12) is nonlinear injective and approximately integrable iff there is a proper 6-tuple HH with m⁡(H)m(H) infinite, such that 𝒢n​[a,b]{\mathcal{G}}_{n}[a{,}b] divides K^1​H\widehat{K}^{1}H.

Proof:

  • ⇐\Leftarrow

    The fact that 𝒢n​[a,b]{\mathcal{G}}_{n}[a{,}b] divides a proper tuple implies that equation (12) is nonlinear injective. The equation is approximately integrable because for every m∈m⁡(H)m\in m(H) there are c,dc,d such that

    S^1=𝒢m​[c,d]H​K^1​H𝒢n​[a,b]\widehat{S}^{1}=\frac{{\mathcal{G}}_{m}[c{,}d]}{H}\frac{\widehat{K}^{1}H}{{\mathcal{G}}_{n}[a{,}b]}

    is proper.

  • ⇒\Rightarrow

    Because equation (12) is nonlinear injective, the tuple S^1=𝒢m​[c,d]​K^1/𝒢n​[a,b]\widehat{S}^{1}={\mathcal{G}}_{m}[c{,}d]\widehat{K}^{1}/{\mathcal{G}}_{n}[a{,}b] is well defined for all mm. The integrability implies that S1S^{1} is proper for infinitely many m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} and c,d∈ℂc,d\in\mathbb{C}. This only happens when 𝒢n=H​P{\mathcal{G}}_{n}=HP factorizes such that P|K^1P\mid\widehat{K}^{1} and m⁡(H)m(H) is infinite. □\square

According to Lemma 2, to classify approximately integrable nonlinear injective equations it suffices to determine the set ℋ6{\mathcal{H}}^{6} of all proper 6-tuples HH with infinite m⁡(H)m(H). This will be done using results from number theory, provided in section 7. In section 8 we determine the proper divisors H∈ℋ1H\in{\mathcal{H}}^{1} of infinitely many functions 𝒢k,mi,1−i{\mathcal{G}}^{i,1-i}_{k,m} for possible i,ki,k. And, in section 9 we determine the proper divisors H∈ℋ2H\in{\mathcal{H}}^{2} of infinitely many 2-tuples 𝒢1,mi,1−i{\mathcal{G}}^{i,1-i}_{1,m}, 𝒢k,mj,1−j{\mathcal{G}}^{j,1-j}_{k,m}, where i≠ji\neq j if k=1k=1. From those results we determine the set ℋ6=⋃n∈ℕℋn6{\mathcal{H}}^{6}=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}{\mathcal{H}}^{6}_{n} in section 10. For each n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} the set ℋn{\mathcal{H}}_{n} is related to the set of approximate integrable equations at order nn, which are not in a lower order hierarchy.

We would like to provide an explicit but minimal list of approximate integrable equations from which one can derive all approximately integrable equations. The following observation is useful. Let PP and QQ be proper tuples. From Lemma 2 it follows that if equation (12), with K^1=P\widehat{K}^{1}=P, is approximately integrable, then the same equation, but with K^1=P​Q\widehat{K}^{1}=PQ, is also approximately integrable. Therefore, the classification in section 10 describes the divisors that have maximal degree. And the corresponding list of equations only contains equations with quadratic parts K1K^{1} of minimal degree.

From the results of sections 8, 9 it follows that ℋn{\mathcal{H}}_{n} is non-empty for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. That means there are new approximately integrable equations at every order. In section 10 we classify the highest degree divisors in ℋn{\mathcal{H}}_{n} completely, that is, for any order. We are not able to explicitly list all corresponding equations, as this paper is bound to be finite. In section 10 we do provide a complete list of approximately integrable equations of order n≤5n\leq 5.

We explicitly provide the linear parts (c​um,d​um)(cu_{m},du_{m}) of all the symmetries of the equations in our list. This enables one to calculate any approximate symmetry in principle. This can be done using Maple code provided at [15]. We remark that if one multiplies the quadratic tuple of an equation with a proper tuple, the resulting equation may have more symmetries than the original one. As we will now illustrate it may also be in a lower hierarchy.

From Lemma 2 we know that if H∈ℋnH\in{\mathcal{H}}_{n} and 𝒢n​[a,b]|K^1​H{\mathcal{G}}_{n}[a{,}b]\mid\widehat{K}^{1}H, then equation (12) is approximately integrable with approximate symmetries at (higher) order m∈m⁡(H)m\in m(H). The following lemma applies.

Lemma 3

Suppose H∈ℋnH\in{\mathcal{H}}_{n} and 𝒢n​[a,b]{\mathcal{G}}_{n}[a{,}b] divides K^1​H\widehat{K}^{1}H. Then equation (12) has more symmetries than the ones at order m∈m⁡(H)m\in m(H) iff there is a divisor Q∈ℋk≤nQ\in{\mathcal{H}}_{k\leq n} of HH, with m⁡(H)m(H) smaller than and contained in m⁡(Q)m(Q), such that 𝒢n​[a,b]{\mathcal{G}}_{n}[a{,}b] divides K^1​Q\widehat{K}^{1}Q.

S^1=𝒢m​[c,d]Q​K^1​Q𝒢n​[a,b].\widehat{S}^{1}=\frac{{\mathcal{G}}_{m}[c{,}d]}{Q}\frac{\widehat{K}^{1}Q}{{\mathcal{G}}_{n}[a{,}b]}.

We need to prove that there is a QQ such that Y=m⁡(Q)Y=m(Q). Take m∈Y∖m⁡(H)m\in Y\setminus m(H) and write 𝒢n=H​P{\mathcal{G}}_{n}=HP. Since 𝒢n|K^1​H{\mathcal{G}}_{n}\mid\widehat{K}^{1}H we have K^1=P​R\widehat{K}^{1}=PR. The tuple S^1=𝒢m​K^1/𝒢n=𝒢m​R/H\widehat{S}^{1}={\mathcal{G}}_{m}\widehat{K}^{1}/{\mathcal{G}}_{n}={\mathcal{G}}_{m}R/H is proper. Since m∉m⁡(H)m\not\in m(H), HH does not divide 𝒢m{\mathcal{G}}_{m}. There is a proper divisor QQ of HH such that Q|𝒢mQ\mid{\mathcal{G}}_{m} and H/QH/Q divides RR, that is, 𝒢n|K^1​Q{\mathcal{G}}_{n}\mid\widehat{K}^{1}Q. Since Q|HQ\mid H the set m⁡(Q)m(Q) is infinite. □\square

Remark 4

One can start with an equation that is not nonlinear injective, multiply its quadratic tuple, and end up in the hierarchy of an nonlinear injective equation. For example, apart from certain purely nonlinear symmetries, equation 1.2 has approximately symmetries with linear part (c​um,d​vm)(cu_{m},dv_{m}) for any c,d∈ℂc,d\in\mathbb{C} when mm is odd. By multiplying its quadratic tuple with the tuple [0,(f1​x1+f2​y1)/f,(y1+y2)/2,0,(i1​x1+i2​y1)/i,(x1+x2)/2][0,(f_{1}x_{1}+f_{2}y_{1})/f,(y_{1}+y_{2})/2,0,(i_{1}x_{1}+i_{2}y_{1})/i,(x_{1}+x_{2})/2] we obtain the equation

(utvt)=(a​u1+f1​u1​v+f2​u​v1+g​v​v1v1+i1​u1​v+i2​u​v1+j​u​u1),\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}au_{1}+f_{1}u_{1}v+f_{2}uv_{1}+gvv_{1}\\ v_{1}+i_{1}u_{1}v+i_{2}uv_{1}+juu_{1}\end{array}\right),

which has approximate symmetries at all orders m>0m>0 for any c,d∈ℂc,d\in\mathbb{C}, and, it is in the hierarchy of an equation of the form 0.3 iff f1=i2=0f_{1}=i_{2}=0. In this paper we do not explicitly describe all symmetries of all approximately integrable equations that can be obtained from our list.

7 Results from number theory

Generally speaking, progress in classifying global classes of evolution equations has been going hand in hand with applying new results or techniques from number theory. For the classification of scalar equations [34] the new result was obtained by F. Beukers, who applied sophisticated techniques from diophantine approximation theory [1]. The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem, stated below, first appeared in the literature in connection with symmetries of evolution equations in [2]. Beukers, Sanders and Wang used a partial corollary of this theorem to conjecture that there are only finitely many integrable equations (12) with K1=[0,0,1,0,0,0]K^{1}=[0,0,1,0,0,0]. Their conjecture became a theorem in [3], where an exhaustive list of the integrable cases was produced using a recent algorithm of C.J. Smyth [4], that solves polynomial equations f⁡(x,y)=0f(x,y)=0 for roots of unity x,yx,y. And, the classification of ℬ{\mathcal{B}}-equations was due to results on diophantine equations in roots of unity, again proved by Beukers [12].

However, as it turns out, we do not need entirely different results or techniques from number theory to globally classify two component evolution equations, with homogeneous diagonal linear part, admitting infinitely many approximate symmetries.

7.1 The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem

A sequence {Um,m∈ℕ}\{U_{m},m\in\mathbb{N}\} satisfies an order nn linear recurrence relation if there exist s1,…,sns_{1},\ldots,s_{n} such that

Um+n=s1Um+n−1+⋯snUm.U_{m+n}=s_{1}U_{m+n-1}+\cdots s_{n}U_{m}.

The general solution can be expressed in terms of a generalized power sum

Um=∑i=1kAi​(m)​αim,U_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}A_{i}(m)\alpha_{i}^{m},

such that the roots αi\alpha_{i} are distinct and non-zero, and the coefficients Ai​(m)A_{i}(m) are polynomial in mm. By definition the degree of UmU_{m} is d=∑i=1kdid=\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}, where did_{i} is the degree of Ai​(m)A_{i}(m). It can be shown that the order of the sequence equals n=k+dn=k+d [32].44 4 In [32] one should replace equation 2.1.2 by equation 1.3 from [33].

A generalized power sum vanishes identically, Um=0U_{m}=0 for all mm, precisely when all its coefficients vanish as polynomials in mm, Ai​(m)=0A_{i}(m)=0 for all ii. We prove this by induction on the degree. For d=0d=0 the statement is plain, the functions h→αihh\rightarrow\alpha_{i}^{h} are linearly independent for distinct αi\alpha_{i}. Let S:f⁡(m)→f⁡(m+1)S:f(m)\rightarrow f(m+1) be the shift operator. Suppose d>0d>0. Then for some ii we have di>0d_{i}>0. The generalized power sum Vm=(S−αi)​UmV_{m}=(S-\alpha_{i})U_{m} has degree d−1d-1. By the induction hypothesis we have, in particular, αi​(S−1)​Ai​(h)=0\alpha_{i}(S-1)A_{i}(h)=0. Since αi≠0\alpha_{i}\neq 0 this implies di=0d_{i}=0 and hence we are done.

Theorem 5 (Skolem–Mahler–Lech)

The zero set of a linear recurrence sequence {m∈ℕ:Um=0}\{m\in\mathbb{N}:U_{m}=0\} is the union of a finite set and finitely many complete arithmetic progressions.

Note that an arithmetic progression pp is complete if p={f+g​h:h∈ℕ}p=\{f+gh:h\in\mathbb{N}\} for some remainder f∈ℕ0f\in\mathbb{N}_{0} and difference g>fg>f, g∈ℕg\in\mathbb{N}. Theorem 5 was first proved by Skolem for the rational numbers [37], by Mahler for algebraic numbers [19], and by Lech for arbitrary fields of characteristic zero [18]. The proofs rely on pp-adic analysis and consist of showing the existence of a difference g∈ℕg\in\mathbb{N} such that every partial sum, with 0≤f<g0\leq f<g,

Uf+g​h=∑i=1k(Ak​(f+g​h)​αif)​(αig)hU_{f+gh}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(A_{k}(f+gh)\alpha_{i}^{f})(\alpha_{i}^{g})^{h} (13)

either has finitely many solutions hh or vanishes identically. We refer to [27, 39], and references in there, for sensible sketches of a proof.

If (13) vanishes identically the sum on the right breaks up into disjoint pieces I⊂{1,…,m}I\subset\{1,\ldots,m\} each of which vanishes because the roots αig\alpha_{i}^{g}, i∈Ii\in I, coincide and the sum of their coefficients ∑i∈IAi​(f+g​h)​αif\sum_{i\in I}A_{i}(f+gh)\alpha_{i}^{f} vanishes identically as a function of the variable hh. Since Ai​(f+g​h)A_{i}(f+gh) does not vanish identically, each piece contains at least two terms. In particular, the following will be usefull.

Corollary 6

If the equation

a1​α1m+a2​α2m+⋯+ak​αkm=0,a_{1}\alpha_{1}^{m}+a_{2}\alpha_{2}^{m}+\cdots+a_{k}\alpha_{k}^{m}=0,

with nonzero ai,αi∈ℂa_{i},\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{C} has infinitely many solutions, the set {α1,α2,…,αk}\{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\} partitions into a number of disjoint subsets, such that each subset has at least two members, and the ratio of any two members of a subset is a root of unity.

For instance, when k=3k=3 the triple α1/α2,α2/α3,α1/α3\alpha_{1}/\alpha_{2},\alpha_{2}/\alpha_{3},\alpha_{1}/\alpha_{3} consists of roots of unity.

7.2 Diophantine equations in roots of unity

The following theorems are of crucial importance for the classification problem considered in this paper.

Theorem 7 (Beukers)

Take m>1m>1 integer. Let μ,ν\mu,\nu be distinct roots of unity, both not equal to 1, such that ν≠μ−1\nu\neq\mu^{-1} when mm is odd. Then

(1−νm)​(1−μ)m=(1−μm)​(1−ν)m(1-\nu^{m})(1-\mu)^{m}=(1-\mu^{m})(1-\nu)^{m} (14)

implies μm=νm=1\mu^{m}=\nu^{m}=1.

Theorem 8 (Beukers)

Take m>1m>1 integer. Let μ,ν\mu,\nu be distinct roots of unity, not both equal to 1, such that ν≠μ−1\nu\neq\mu^{-1} when mm is even. Then

(1+νm)​(1−μ)m=(1+μm)​(1−ν)m(1+\nu^{m})(1-\mu)^{m}=(1+\mu^{m})(1-\nu)^{m} (15)

implies μm=νm=−1\mu^{m}=\nu^{m}=-1.

Theorem 9 (Beukers)

Take m>1m>1 integer. Let μ,ν\mu,\nu be roots of unity with μ≠1\mu\neq 1. Then

(1+νm)​(1−μ)m=(1−μm)​(1−ν)m(1+\nu^{m})(1-\mu)^{m}=(1-\mu^{m})(1-\nu)^{m} (16)

implies μm=−νm=1\mu^{m}=-\nu^{m}=1.

Whereas the Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem implies that certain ratios are roots of unity for the equation to have infinitely many solutions, the above theorems tell us precisely what the solutions are. In particular, they imply that the zero sets consist of complete arithmetic progressions only.

Theorems 7,8,9 are slightly more general than [12, Theorems 22,25], which were proved by F. Beukers. We won’t repeat their proofs here, however we do indicate the difference between the two sets of Theorems, which is twofold. Firstly, in Theorems 7,8,9 we do not assume that μ,ν≠−1\mu,\nu\neq-1. In certain cases this follows from [12, Proposition 24], in others one has to rely on the following.

Proposition 10 (Beukers)

If ν\nu is a root of unity such that

(1+νm)​2m−1=(1−ν)m,(1+\nu^{m})2^{m-1}=(1-\nu)^{m}, (17)

then ν=−1\nu=-1 and mm is even.

Proof: By Galois theory we may assume that ν=e2​π​i/n\nu=e^{2\pi i/n}. Taking n=1n=1 does not give any solutions. If n=2n=2 then mm has to be even. We will show there are no solutions with n>2n>2. When m=1m=1 there is no root of unity such that 1+ν=1−ν1+\nu=1-\nu. Taking m=2m=2 it follows that n=2n=2. So we may assume that m>2m>2.

Since ν≠1\nu\neq 1, |1+νm||1+\nu^{m}| does not vanish and we have |1+νm|>sin⁡(π/n)|1+\nu^{m}|>\sin(\pi/n). Also we use |1−ν|<2​π/n|1-\nu|<2\pi/n. This gives

(2​πn)m>|1−ν|m=|1+νm|​2m−1>sin⁡(πn)​2m−1.(2\frac{\pi}{n})^{m}>|1-\nu|^{m}=|1+\nu^{m}|2^{m-1}>\sin(\frac{\pi}{n})2^{m-1}.

Division by 2m​π/n2^{m}\pi/n yields (taking n>2n>2)

(πn)m−1>sin⁡(πn)​n2​π>.41,(\frac{\pi}{n})^{m-1}>\sin(\frac{\pi}{n})\frac{n}{2\pi}>.41,

which implies (taking m>2m>2) that π/n>.64\pi/n>.64, or n<5n<5. When n=3n=3, |1+νm||1+\nu^{m}| equals 1 or 2, and |1−ν|=3|1-\nu|=\sqrt{3}, whose mm-th power does not equal 2m2^{m} or 2m−12^{m-1}. When n=4n=4, |1+νm||1+\nu^{m}| equals 0 or 2\sqrt{2} or 22, and |1−ν|=2|1-\nu|=\sqrt{2}, whose mm-th power, with m>1m>1, does not equal 00 or 2​2m−1\sqrt{2}2^{m-1} or 2m2^{m}. □\square

Secondly in the proofs we do not in general need ν≠μ\nu\neq\mu and ν≠1/μ\nu\neq 1/\mu. And, we also note that in [12, Theorem 25] it was mistakenly supposed that μn≠−1\mu^{n}\neq-1. This should have been μn≠∓1\mu^{n}\neq\mp 1 depending on the sign in [12, equation (10)].

8 Homogeneous quadratic parts

In this section we determine the proper divisors of infinitely many 1-tuples 𝒢m=𝒢k,mi,1−i{\mathcal{G}}_{m}={\mathcal{G}}^{i,1-i}_{k,m} for all possible choices of i,ki,k.

Due to equation (10) we may take k=1k=1; equations of the form (ut,vt)=(a​un,b​vn+K)(u_{t},v_{t})=(au_{n},bv_{n}+K) are related, by the linear transformation u↔vu\leftrightarrow v, to equations of the form (ut,vt)=(a​un+K,b​vn)(u_{t},v_{t})=(au_{n}+K,bv_{n}). We start with the simplest case i=1i=1.

8.1 Classifying approximately integrable scalar equations

The Lie derivative of the quadratic part S1S^{1} of a possible scalar symmetry with respect to the linear part K0=unK^{0}=u_{n} of a scalar equation ut=K0+K1+⋯u_{t}=K^{0}+K^{1}+\cdots is symbolically given by ℒ⁡(K0)​S1​⊵​Gn1​S^1{\mathcal{L}}(K^{0})S^{1}\trianglerighteq G^{1}_{n}\widehat{S}^{1} with 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}-function

𝒢n1​(x,y)=xn+yn−(x+y)n=𝒢1;n1,0​[a,b]​(x,y)/a.{\mathcal{G}}^{1}_{n}(x,y)=x^{n}+y^{n}-(x+y)^{n}={\mathcal{G}}^{1,0}_{1;n}[a{,}b](x,y)/a.

Thus the case i=k=1i=k=1 is equivalent to the scalar problem, which is easily seen by taking v=0v=0. The function is also proportional to 𝒢k,ni,1−i​[a,a]{\mathcal{G}}^{i,1-i}_{k,n}[a{,}a] so the results apply to the case a=ba=b as well.

In the classification of scalar equations [34] a different route was taken than the one we take. Namely, whereas we perform our classification with respect to the existence of infinitely many (approximate) symmetries, Sanders and Wang performed their classification with respect to the existence of symmetries (finitely many or infinitely many). They showed in particular that there are no scalar equations with finitely many generalized symmetries, which confirms the first part of the conjecture of Fokas [8]:

If a scalar equation possesses at least one time-independent non-Lie point symmetry, then it possesses infinitely many. Similarly for NN-component equations one needs NN symmetries.

We note that the conjecture of Fokas does not hold inside the class of ℬ{\mathcal{B}}-equations [16]. In their classification Sanders and Wang relied on the following ‘hard to obtain’ result from number theory, proved in [1].

Theorem 11 (Beukers)

Let r∈ℂr\in\mathbb{C} such that r⁡(r+1)​(r2+r+1)≠0r(r+1)(r^{2}+r+1)\neq 0. Then at most one integer m>1m>1 exists such that 𝒢m1​(1,r)=0{\mathcal{G}}^{1}_{m}(1,r)=0.

In contrast, classifying the equations with respect to (approximate) integrability can be done using the following ‘easy to obtain’ result. Proposition 12 is of course not as strong as Theorem 11. For obvious reasons we do not include the constant divisors in ℋ0{\mathcal{H}}_{0} in our lists.

The proper divisors of infinitely many 𝒢1;m1,0​[c,d]​(1,y){\mathcal{G}}^{1,0}_{1;m}[c{,}d](1,y) are products of

    (1+y)∈ℋ3(1+y)\in{\mathcal{H}}_{3}, m≡1mod2m\equiv 1\mod 2

  3. 3.

    1+y+y2∈ℋ51+y+y^{2}\in{\mathcal{H}}_{5}, m≡1,5mod6m\equiv 1,5\mod 6

  4. 4.

    (1+y+y2)2∈ℋ7(1+y+y^{2})^{2}\in{\mathcal{H}}_{7}, m≡1mod6m\equiv 1\mod 6

The orders are found by substituting the values for rr. We have 𝒢m1​(1,0)=0{\mathcal{G}}^{1}_{m}(1,0)=0 for all mm, 𝒢f+2​h1​(1,−1)=1+(−1)f=0{\mathcal{G}}^{1}_{f+2h}(1,-1)=1+(-1)^{f}=0 when f=1f=1, and, with 1+r+r2=01+r+r^{2}=0, 𝒢f+6​h1​(1,r)=1+rf−(1+r)f=0{\mathcal{G}}^{1}_{f+6h}(1,r)=1+r^{f}-(1+r)^{f}=0 when f=1f=1 or f=5f=5. As a particular corollary of Proposition 12 we have the following. Equation (12) with a=ba=b and n=2,3,5,7n=2,3,5,7 is approximately integrable for arbitrary K1K^{1}.

Lemma 16

Suppose that the diophantine equation (26), with A​B​C≠0ABC\neq 0, has infinitely many solutions. Then AA, BB, and CC are roots of unity.

Proof: Using Corollary 6, three of the numbers 1,A,B,A​B,C1,A,B,AB,C have a root of unity as a ratio and the same is true for the remaining two. Therefore at least one of the pairs C,AC,A; C,BC,B; C/A,BC/A,B; C/B,AC/B,A consists of roots of unity. When CC and AA are roots of unity, their powers yield a finite number of values. Moreover, for the infinite number of solutions we have (1+a​Am)≠0(1+aA^{m})\neq 0. Hence, for these infinite number of solutions (1+b​Bm)(1+bB^{m}) has only finitely many values. This only happens when BB is a root of unity. The other cases lead to the same result, e.g. when C/AC/A and BB are roots of unity we divide the equation by AmA^{m} and find that AA is a root of unity. □\square

Suppose that the triple ζ,η,f⁡(ζ,η)\zeta,\eta,f(\zeta,\eta) consist of roots of unity. In particular, a finite number of values will be obtained. We denote the set of all primitive nn-th roots of unity by Φn′\Phi^{\prime}_{n}.

10 Global classification of maximal degree divisors

Combining the results obtained in Propositions 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19 we determine the set of all highest degree proper 6-tuples with infinite m⁡(H)m(H). This is equivalent to a global classification of approximately integrable two-component equations with a diagonal linear part, see section 6. Highest degree tuples are formed as follows. With H∈ℋnH\in{\mathcal{H}}_{n} and F∈ℋkF\in{\mathcal{H}}_{k} we have H​F∈ℋlHF\in{\mathcal{H}}_{l}, where ll is the smallest number in m⁡(H​F)=m⁡(H)∩m⁡(F)m(HF)=m(H)\cap m(F).

Clearly if HH divides 𝒢m​[c,d]{\mathcal{G}}_{m}[c,d] then HH divides 𝒢m​[c/d,1]{\mathcal{G}}_{m}[c/d,1]. Also, if

H=[O⁡(x1,x2),P⁡(x1,y1),Q⁡(y1,y2),R⁡(y1,y2),S⁡(x1,y1),T⁡(x1,x2)]H=[O(x_{1},x_{2}),P(x_{1},y_{1}),Q(y_{1},y_{2}),R(y_{1},y_{2}),S(x_{1},y_{1}),T(x_{1},x_{2})]

divides 𝒢m​[c,1]{\mathcal{G}}_{m}[c,1] then, according to equation (10), the function 𝒢m​[1/c,1]{\mathcal{G}}_{m}[1/c,1] admits the proper divisor

H†=[R⁡(x1,x2),S⁡(y1,x1),T⁡(y1,y2),O⁡(y1,y2),P⁡(y1,x1),Q⁡(x1,x2)].H^{\dagger}=[R(x_{1},x_{2}),S(y_{1},x_{1}),T(y_{1},y_{2}),O(y_{1},y_{2}),P(y_{1},x_{1}),Q(x_{1},x_{2})].

Thus we scale dd in 𝒢m​[c,d]{\mathcal{G}}_{m}[c,d] to 1, and perform the classification up to inversion of cc.

We also include tuples with zero components in the list. They correspond to equations that are not nonlinear injective, see section 5. For each K0K^{0} in Table 1 we have determined the highest degree rr-tuple HH, with m⁡(H)m(H) infinite, which divides the rr-tuple consisting of the non-zero components of its 𝒢n{\mathcal{G}}_{n}-tuple. The quadratic tuple K1K^{1} has rr non-zero components K1=𝒢n/HK^{1}={\mathcal{G}}_{n}/H, unless complementary components of the 𝒢m{\mathcal{G}}_{m}-tuple vanish at infinitely m∈m⁡(H)m\in m(H).

First we deal with ℋn≤56{\mathcal{H}}^{6}_{n\leq 5}. Here we translate our symbolic results into differential language. For any H∈ℋnH\in{\mathcal{H}}_{n} of highest degree, which divides 𝒢n​[a,1]{\mathcal{G}}_{n}[a,1], we determine K1K^{1} from K^1=[e,f,g,h,i,j]​𝒢n​[a,1]/H\widehat{K}^{1}=[e,f,g,h,i,j]{\mathcal{G}}_{n}[a,1]/H. In principal, the tuple [e,f,g,h,i,j][e,f,g,h,i,j] may consist of proper polynomials, it is a common factor of K^1\widehat{K}^{1} and S1^\widehat{S^{1}}. However, when writing down the differential equation, the e,f,g,h,i,je,f,g,h,i,j will appear in it as constants, and any other constants will be absorbed by them. This organizes the quadratic part of the equations. At the same time it may remind the reader of the fact that the quadratic tuple of the equations can be multiplied by arbitrary proper tuples. We give each maximal degree tuple H∈ℋnH\in{\mathcal{H}}_{n} two indices, H=Hn.hH=H_{n.h}, where nn is the order, and hh is a counter. We label the corresponding approximately integrable equation by n.hn.h. And, we express the linear coefficients c/dc/d of the approximate symmetries in terms of integer sequences, or in its power sum solution if that displays well.

Secondly we give a general description of ℋn>56{\mathcal{H}}^{6}_{n>5}. Using this result one can, in principle, write down the corresponding approximate integrable systems at any particular order. Some Maple code has been provided at [15].

11 Concluding remarks

In the formal symmetry approach [25], as well as in the computer-assisted schemes [9, 40], not knowing the ratios of eigenvalues strongly complicates the classification of integrable equations. There the ratios are obtained, if possible at all, at the very last stage of the calculations. We hope that the a priori knowledge provided in this article will be an impetus to complete the classification.

Usually, in classification programs one considers homogeneous equations. A 2-component equation (ut,vt)=K(u_{t},v_{t})=K is homogeneous of weighting λ\lambda if KK is an eigenvector of ℒ⁡(σx+λ1​σu+λ2​σv){\mathcal{L}}(\sigma_{x}+\lambda_{1}\sigma_{u}+\lambda_{2}\sigma_{v}), where σx=(x​u1,x​v1)\sigma_{x}=(xu_{1},xv_{1}) counts the number of derivatives. We have compactly provided a list of nonhomogeneous equations. A complete list of homogeneous equations can be obtained from our list by multiplying the symbolic quadratic parts with appropriate tuples of polynomials. And Lemma 3 can be used to determine all symmetries of those equations.

A classification of second order integrable 2-component evolution equations has been given in [35]. The lemmas 6.3, 6.4, 6.5, and 6.6, proved in there, are special cases (n=2n=2) of Proposition 15, 18, 19, and 17, respectively. In [35] the full analysis of higher order symmetry conditions was carried out completely. From this it follows that all second order integrable equations with quadratic parts are derived from equations 2.3, 2.4, and 2.5. Note that the authors of [35] excluded equations of type 2.1 and 2.2.

A classification of third order 2-component evolution equations with weighting (2,2)(2,2) and symmetries of order 5, 7, or 9, is given in [9]. Of the five equations listed [9, Theorem 3.3], two are nonlinear injective and have diagonalizable linear part:

(utvt)=(u3+u​u1+v​v1−2​v3−u​v1)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{3}+uu_{1}+vv_{1}\\ -2v_{3}-uv_{1}\end{array}\right) (38)

and

(utvt)=(4​u3+3​v3+4​u​u1+v​u1+2​u​v13​u3+v3−2​v​v1−4​v​u1−2​u​v1).\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}4u_{3}+3v_{3}+4uu_{1}+vu_{1}+2uv_{1}\\ 3u_{3}+v_{3}-2vv_{1}-4vu_{1}-2uv_{1}\end{array}\right). (39)

When put in Jordan form the ratio of the coefficients of the linear part of equation (39) becomes a/b=−3​ϕ−2a/b=-3\phi-2, where ϕ\phi is the golden ratio. Our diophantine approach perfectly explains the ’unusual’ symmetry pattern. We remark that the conjugate of ϕ\phi gives rise to another equation with a/b=−3​(1−ϕ)−2=1/(−3​ϕ−2)a/b=-3(1-\phi)-2=1/(-3\phi-2), which can be obtained by interchanging uu and vv. A similar remark holds for all equations derived from the ’symmetric’ Propositions 18 and 19. For example, by interchanging uu and vv in equation 4.11 we get an equation with a/b=1/(7+4​γ)=7−4​γa/b=1/(7+4\gamma)=7-4\gamma.

According to [9, Theorem 3.3] we have the following. A non-decouplable fifth order two component equation in the KDV weighting, possessing a generalized symmetry of order 7 can be reduced by a linear change of variables to a symmetry of lower order equations, or to the Zhou-Jiang-Jiang equation,

(utvt)=(u5−5​(2​u​u3+5​u1​u2)+15​(2​v​v3+3​v1​v2)+20​u1​u2−30​(u1​v2+2​u​v​v1)−9​v5+5​(2​u3​v+7​u2​v1+9​u1​v2+6​u​v3)−10​(2​u​u1​vCLOSEOPEN+2​u2​v1+3​v2​v1)).\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\begin{split}u_{5}-5(2uu_{3}+5u_{1}u_{2})+15(2vv_{3}+3v_{1}v_{2})+20u_{1}u^{2}\\ -30(u_{1}v^{2}+2uvv_{1})\end{split}\\ \begin{split}-9v_{5}+5(2u_{3}v+7u_{2}v_{1}+9u_{1}v_{2}+6uv_{3})-10(2uu_{1}v\\ +2u^{2}v_{1}+3v^{2}v_{1})\end{split}\end{array}\right).

However, since the ratio of coefficients of the linear part a/b=−1/9a/b=-1/9 does not appear in our list, this equation has an approximate symmetry at lower order. In fact, the equation has a genuine symmetry at third order. The Zhou-Jiang-Jiang equation is in the hierarchy of the Drinfeld-Sokolov type [7] equation

(utvt)=(−3​v​v1v3−u1​v−2​u​v1),\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}-3vv_{1}\\ v_{3}-u_{1}v-2uv_{1}\end{array}\right), (40)

which is linearly equivalent to a third order equation that appears in the same paper [9, Equation (17)], cf. [40, Sections 3.2.1, 4.2.6]. The special value of the ratio a/b=−1/2a/b=-1/2 in equation (38) also does not appear in our list and is due to higher grading constraints. At the end of [24] two fifth order systems are given with ratios (9−5​3)​(9+5​3)−1=26−15​3(9-5\sqrt{3})(9+5\sqrt{3})^{-1}=26-15\sqrt{3} and −1/9-1/9. The first system derives from equation 5.6 and the latter from equation 5.3, with rr a primitive 66-th root of unity.

We conclude with a more philosophical remark and some ideas on future research. The concept of generalized symmetry really is about local symmetry. The (inverse) Gel’fand-Dikiĭ transformation translates polynomials in the symbols x,yx,y into local differential functions, that is expressions in u,vu,v and their derivatives. A question arises: can we also translate rational functions in the symbols x,yx,y? The answer is yes. One could think of non-local variables ui,viu_{i},v_{i} with 0>i∈ℤ0>i\in\mathbb{Z}. Here a negative index indicates integration and DxD_{x} would be such that Dx​(ui−1)=uiD_{x}(u_{i-1})=u_{i} for all ii. We can expand rational functions in Taylor-series, which are transformed into non-local differential sums. For example, consider the rational function F^=1/(x1+x2)\widehat{F}=1/(x_{1}+x_{2}). Its symmetric Taylor-series is

F^=12​∑k=0∞(−1)k​(x1kx2k+1+x2kx1k+1)\widehat{F}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{k}(\frac{x_{1}^{k}}{x_{2}^{k+1}}+\frac{x_{2}^{k}}{x_{1}^{k+1}})

which is transformed into the non-local object

F=∑k=0∞(−1)k​uk​u−k−1,F=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{k}u_{k}u_{-k-1},

and we have Dx​F=u2D_{x}F=u^{2}. In this non-local setting every equation has a symmetry at any order. For example, the equation, with a≠1a\neq 1,

(utvt)=(a​u1+(1−a)​u​vv1+(1−a)​u​v),\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}au_{1}+(1-a)uv\\ v_{1}+(1-a)uv\end{array}\right),

and its approximate symmetries (but the ones in 𝒜2,0⊗𝒜0,2{\mathcal{A}}^{2,0}\otimes{\mathcal{A}}^{0,2}), are in the approximate hierarchy of the zeroth order non-local equation

(utvt)=(u+u​v−1v−u−1​v).\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u+uv_{-1}\\ v-u_{-1}v\end{array}\right).

Still, there would be a quest for equations, or symmetries, that are in certain sense close to local.

Since the pioneering work of Sanders and Wang [34], apart from extending the result to equations with more more components [3, 35, 12], the symbolic method has been further developed in order to classify non-commutative [30], non-evolutionary [21, 23, 28], non-local [21, 22], and multi-dimensional equations [41]. In classifying non-local equations the concept of quasi-locality, introduced in [26] is the key idea. Only certain types of non-localities are allowed by considering different extensions of the ring of differential polynomials. ‘Nnon-evolutionary’ equations are treated as evolution equations with possible non-localities. For example, a Boussinesq type scalar equation

ut​t=K⁡(u,ux,ux​x​…,ut,ux​t,…CLOSEu_{tt}=K(u,u_{x},u_{xx}\ldots,u_{t},u_{xt},\ldots

can be represented as a two-component evolution equation,

(utvt)=(vK⁡(u,ux,…,v,vx,…)).\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}v\\ K(u,u_{x},\ldots,v,v_{x},\ldots)\end{array}\right).

However, different evolutionary representation may exist, and some might have local symmetries, whereas others might posses non-local symmetries [23]. Another example is the Camassa-Holm type equation

(mtux​x)=(c​m​ux+u​mxu−m),\left(\begin{array}[]{c}m_{t}\\ u_{xx}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}cmu_{x}+um_{x}\\ u-m\end{array}\right),

which is integrable when c=2c=2 [5] and c=3c=3 [6]. By eliminating the variable uu this equation is written as

mt=c​m​Δ​mx+mx​Δ​mm_{t}=cm\Delta m_{x}+m_{x}\Delta m

where Δ=(1−Dx2)−1\Delta=(1-D_{x}^{2})^{-1} is a non-local operator. Its symmetries are quasi-local expressions in DxD_{x}-, and Δ\Delta-derivatives of mm [21, 24].

Another interesting problem would be to classify non-evolutionary equations as they are, that is, to apply the symbolic method for polynomials in both xx and tt derivatives, developed in [41]. In the setting of non-evolutionary equations, there is a clear distinction between the equation and its symmetries. When Δ=0\Delta=0 represents the equation, a function QQ is an infinitesimal symmetry if the prolongation of QQ acting on Δ\Delta vanishes modulo Δ\Delta [29, Theorem 2.31]. For example, we have ut​x​x−ut​uxu_{txx}-u_{t}u_{x} as a symmetry of the Boussinesq equation ut​t=ux​x​x​x−2​ux​ux​xu_{tt}=u_{xxxx}-2u_{x}u_{xx}, but not vise versa. Recently we formulated an equivalent symmetry condition in terms of Lie-brackets, in the setting of passive orthonomic systems [14]. This could play a role in the general classification problem. We also found that certain hierarchies of evolution equations appear as symmetries of non-evolutionary equations. For example, it seems that all symmetries of the Sawada-Kotera equation [36]

ut=u5−5​u3​u1+53​w13u_{t}=u_{5}-5u_{3}u_{1}+\frac{5}{3}w_{1}^{3}

are symmetries of ut​x​x=ut​uxu_{txx}=u_{t}u_{x}, which is a special case of Ito’s equation [31]. Based on Lax-pairs a similar observation was made in [11].
